siteItem.title: Check the next headline you see
siteItem.text: Before you share a story on this topic, see how it rates on hype and evidence.

footer: We don’t tell you which side to take, only how to be heard. Speaking up doesn’t guarantee an outcome.

water.intro: One AI answer doesn’t use up a whole bottle of water. The real concern is local: big data centers can strain water supplies in some dry towns, especially on the hottest days. Here’s how to act on that.

learn.title: Find out where your water comes from
learn.text: Your yearly water quality report names the river, lake or aquifer your water comes from, plus a phone number for your water system.

speakUp.title: Contact your state lawmakers
speakUp.text: Tell your state legislators what you think about data centers and water, whichever side you’re on.

speakUp.title: Comment on a draft water permit
speakUp.text: When a facility applies for a permit to release wastewater, the public must be told and allowed to comment. Watch your local paper for notices.

takeAction.title: Go to your city council meeting
takeAction.text: Ask your city or county when a data center plan will be voted on and how much water it would need, then speak during public comment.

takeAction.title: Team up with your neighbors
takeAction.text: Gather neighbors to study a proposal and comment together. In Tucson, over a thousand residents weighed in before the city set data center water rules.

jobs.intro: No one knows if AI will take every job, and so far there’s no clear sign of widespread job loss in the US. The real concerns are fewer entry-level openings in some fields and how work is changing. Here’s how to act on those.

learn.title: Learn what AI job ratings mean
learn.text: The Bureau of Labor Statistics explains how it rates the overlap between AI and each job’s tasks, and why a high rating doesn’t mean a job will vanish.

speakUp.title: Contact your members of Congress
speakUp.text: Congress funds job training and sets national work rules. Tell your US representative and senators what you think about AI and jobs, whichever side you’re on.

speakUp.title: Raise AI questions with coworkers
speakUp.text: Federal law protects many workers who talk with coworkers about pay and working conditions. You can bring questions about AI changes to your employer together.

takeAction.title: Weigh in with your workforce board
takeAction.text: Ask your local workforce board how it’s preparing workers for AI and how the public can give input.

takeAction.title: Help someone find free job help
takeAction.text: American Job Centers offer free help with job searches and training. Go yourself, or bring a friend or neighbor who has lost work.

existential-risk.intro: Nobody has shown that AI will wipe out humanity, and nobody has shown it can’t. The real questions are how the most powerful AI systems get tested and who oversees them. Here’s how to act on those.

learn.title: Read the international expert report
learn.text: More than 100 experts from over 30 countries laid out what today’s AI can do and where they still disagree about serious risks.

speakUp.title: Contact your members of Congress
speakUp.text: Ask what they plan to do about testing and oversight of the most powerful AI. Share your view, whichever side you’re on.

speakUp.title: Weigh in on state AI rules
speakUp.text: California now requires the biggest makers of advanced AI to publish safety plans. Ask your own state lawmakers where they stand and tell them what you think.

takeAction.title: Go to a town hall meeting
takeAction.text: Check your representative’s website for town halls or local office hours. Go with neighbors and ask how they would handle risks from powerful AI.

takeAction.title: Ask questions at work or school
takeAction.text: Team up with coworkers or parents and use NIST’s voluntary AI risk guide to ask who approves AI tools and who fixes problems.

data-centers.intro: Data centers aren’t destroying whole towns. The real questions are who pays for the power, how much noise neighbors live with, and whether the tax breaks are worth it. Here’s how to act on those.

learn.title: Read the most detailed official study
learn.text: Virginia’s 2024 state audit looked at power bills, noise, water and tax breaks.

speakUp.title: Contact your state lawmakers
speakUp.text: States decide data center tax breaks and power rules. Tell your state legislators what you think, whichever side you’re on.

speakUp.title: Ask your utility commission who pays
speakUp.text: Ask whether large data centers cover the cost of the new power lines and plants built for them.

takeAction.title: Show up at the hearing
takeAction.text: Ask your county or city planning office for the site plan and the date of the zoning vote, then speak during public comment.

takeAction.title: Team up with neighbors
takeAction.text: Start a petition or local group, or organize a peaceful gathering. Towns in Missouri and Kansas have done it.

energy-climate.intro: AI won’t necessarily make climate change worse, but its growing power use can raise emissions where the grid still runs on gas or coal. The real questions are what power gets built and who pays. Here’s how to act on those.

learn.title: Check how your area makes power
learn.text: Enter your ZIP code in EPA’s Power Profiler to compare emissions from your local power plants with the national average.

speakUp.title: Comment on your utility’s plans
speakUp.text: State utility commissions review plans for new power plants and set rates. Ask yours for the case number on data center demand, then file a comment.

speakUp.title: Get help with federal energy cases
speakUp.text: FERC’s Office of Public Participation helps people find filings and deadlines and explains how to comment on federal power matters.

takeAction.title: Show up at the local hearing
takeAction.text: Ask your city or county when it will vote on a data center or new power plant, then speak during public comment, whichever side you’re on.

takeAction.title: Join a community solar project
takeAction.text: Community solar lets neighbors, including renters, share power from one solar array and get credit on their bills. Ask your utility what’s offered.

creativity.intro: Calling AI art “theft” goes further than the facts, and US courts haven’t settled whether training on others’ work is legal. The real questions are whether creators should be asked and paid, and how to protect your own work. Here’s how to act on those.

learn.title: Read the official AI copyright reports
learn.text: The US Copyright Office studied AI training, digital copies of real people, and whether AI-made work can be copyrighted in a three-part series.

speakUp.title: Tell Congress what you think
speakUp.text: Congress writes copyright law, including any rules on AI training, consent or pay. Contact your US senators and representative, whichever side you’re on.

speakUp.title: File a low-cost copyright claim
speakUp.text: If a specific work of yours was copied, this federal board is a cheaper option than court. Awards are capped at $30,000, and the other side can opt out.

takeAction.title: Register the work you care about
takeAction.text: You own the copyright as soon as you make something, but you must register a US work before you can sue anyone over it.

takeAction.title: Team up with other creators
takeAction.text: Join or start a group of artists to share what you learn and act together. Three artists joined forces to take their concerns to court.

privacy.intro: ChatGPT isn’t posting your chats for other people to read. The real issues are whether your chats help train the AI, who at the company can see them, and that no outside audit checks the rules. Here’s how to act on those.

learn.title: Read OpenAI’s own data rules
learn.text: OpenAI’s help page explains who can look at your chats and why, how deleting works, and what it asks you not to share.

speakUp.title: Tell lawmakers what privacy you expect
speakUp.text: Congress and state legislatures decide what privacy rights you have with tech companies. Tell your lawmakers what you think, whichever side you’re on.

speakUp.title: Use your privacy rights
speakUp.text: If you live in California, you can ask a company what personal data it has about you and ask it to delete that data.

takeAction.title: Turn off training in your settings
takeAction.text: In ChatGPT, open Settings, then Data controls, and switch off “Improve the model for everyone.” Thumbs-up or thumbs-down feedback can still be used.

takeAction.title: Ask for clear rules at work
takeAction.text: Team up with coworkers, or other parents at your school, to ask which AI accounts are approved and who can read those chats. On business accounts, admins may see them.
